blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — home sharps disposal
stem: A client self-administers insulin at home. Which instruction about used needles is appropriate?

options.A: Place each used needle promptly into a sharps disposal container; use an FDA-cleared container when available and follow community disposal rules.
options.B: Place capped used needles in a sturdy household trash bag after each injection, then discard the sealed bag with ordinary household waste.
options.C: Keep used needles in a covered tray until several accumulate, then transfer them together into a sharps container to reduce container changes.
options.D: Place used needles in a rigid recycling container after injection, then send the sealed container through the household recycling program.

rationale: A is correct. Current FDA guidance recommends immediately placing used needles and other sharps into a sharps disposal container. FDA-cleared containers are recommended when available; if one is unavailable, an appropriate heavy-duty plastic household container may be an alternative under applicable community guidance. Filled sharps containers should be disposed of according to local or community requirements. B is unsafe because loose or merely capped sharps should not go into ordinary household trash. C delays prompt containment and creates avoidable handling of accumulated sharps. D is incorrect because needles and other sharps should not be placed in household recycling.
educational_objective: Teach home users to place used needles immediately into an appropriate sharps container and dispose of the filled container according to local or community requirements.
source_organization: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA); National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_document_title: Best Way to Get Rid of Used Needles and Other Sharps; Sharps Disposal Containers; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: Current FDA consumer sharps guidance live-rechecked 2026-08-21; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: FDA Best Way to Get Rid of Used Needles and Other Sharps, Step 1: place all needles and other sharps in a sharps disposal container immediately after use; Step 2: dispose of used sharps containers according to community guidelines. FDA Sharps Disposal Containers: FDA-cleared containers are recommended; if unavailable, an appropriate heavy-duty plastic household container may be used as an alternative; when about three-quarters full, follow community disposal guidelines.
source_claim_supported: Current FDA guidance directly supports immediate sharps-container placement, preference for FDA-cleared containers when available, acceptable heavy-duty household alternatives when appropriate, and disposal according to community requirements.
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control, printed p.8: handle biohazardous materials safely, prevent injury, and provide safety/infection-prevention teaching.
pdf_visual_verification: PASS — the official 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan Safety and Infection Prevention and Control page was screenshot-verified earlier in this continuation; the home-sharps clinical claims are supported by current FDA HTML.

option_audit.A: Correct; matches FDA immediate containment and community-disposal guidance without implying FDA-cleared containers are the only permissible option.
option_audit.B: Plausible household-disposal shortcut but incorrect because loose or capped sharps should not be placed in ordinary household trash.
option_audit.C: Plausible convenience strategy but incorrect because FDA recommends immediate placement rather than accumulating sharps for later transfer.
option_audit.D: Plausible rigid-container idea but incorrect because sharps should not enter household recycling programs.

cueing_audit.answer_length: Final option lengths are balanced: A 145, B 139, C 142, D 139 characters; the key is not conspicuously longer.
cueing_audit.absolute_words: No distractor depends on a simplistic always/never/only cue.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: No defensible second answer identified: B uses household trash for individual sharps, C delays immediate containment, and D routes sharps into recycling.
